                    ### Question
                    A six year-old female presents for evaluation of dry skin, fatigue, sensitivity to cold and constipation. The patient’s mother recalls that the patient had surgery to remove a “benign mass” at the base of her tongue 3 months ago because of trouble swallowing. What was the likely cause of the surgically removed mass?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Maternal Diabetes Mellitus
opb. Radiation exposure
opc. Iodine deficiency
opd. Failed caudal migration of the thyroid gland
ope. Failed fusion of the palatine shelves with the nasal septum

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The symptoms of dry skin, fatigue, sensitivity to cold, and constipation are indicative of hypothyroidism, which is consistent with thyroid dysfunction. The mass at the base of the tongue is likely ectopic thyroid tissue, known as a lingual thyroid, resulting from the failed caudal migration of the thyroid gland during development. This aligns with the consensus that the thyroid gland originates at the base of the tongue and migrates down to the neck; failure in this process can lead to ectopic thyroid tissue. The retrieved evidence paths support the link between hypothyroidism symptoms and thyroid dysfunction, reinforcing the reasoning that the mass was due to failed caudal migration of the thyroid gland. Therefore, the most likely cause of the surgically removed mass is the failed caudal migration of the thyroid gland.
